questions.question: Name the four factors of production with their rewards, and use one characteristic of each factor to explain why it is paid the way it is.
questions.expected_answer: Natural resources earn rent, labour earns wages and salaries, capital earns interest, and entrepreneurship earns profit. Natural resources are fixed in total supply and cannot be produced, so quantity supplied cannot respond to price and rent is set almost entirely by demand — the corner trading site is expensive because many traders want that exact spot and nobody can make another. Labour is inseparable from the worker and perishable, so it is hired as a continuing service at a negotiated wage, with collective bargaining, the national minimum wage as the floor and productivity as the ceiling shaping the figure. Capital is produced through saving and investment and it depreciates, so its reward is interest — the price of the funds that acquired it, moved by the repo rate, risk and term. Entrepreneurship organises the other factors and carries the uninsurable risk that customers never arrive, so its reward, profit, is the residual paid last, which can be negative — and bearing that risk is exactly why the entrepreneur holds the right to decide.

questions.question: A Pietermaritzburg furniture factory sells R6 000 000 of output and buys in R2 400 000 of timber, fabric, electricity and transport. It pays wages of R2 250 000, rent of R330 000 and interest of R270 000, and sets aside R270 000 for consumption of fixed capital. Calculate value added and profit, and explain why the bought-in items are excluded from the share-out.
questions.expected_answer: Value added is output minus intermediate purchases: R6 000 000 minus R2 400 000 gives R3 600 000. The contractual payments — wages R2 250 000, rent R330 000, interest R270 000 and depreciation R270 000 — total R3 120 000, so profit as the residual is R3 600 000 minus R3 120 000, which is R480 000. Adding all five slices back returns exactly R3 600 000, which is the check. The R2 400 000 of timber, fabric, electricity and transport is intermediate consumption, not a factor payment: those inputs already generated wages, rent, interest and profit inside the sawmill, the mill and the utility that supplied them, so counting them again in this firm's value added would count the same income twice. Depreciation, in turn, is income to nobody — it is capital being used up and reserved for replacement — so net value added is R3 330 000.

questions.question: Explain how local economic planning, accessibility for marginalised groups, community participation and empowerment procurement work together to widen access to the factors of production in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Local economic planning flows from local government's constitutional object of promoting development: every municipality adopts and annually revisits an Integrated Development Plan, whose economic heart is a factor question — what does this place hold in land, minerals, infrastructure and skills, and how can those factors be combined here instead of being exported raw? Accessibility identifies who is shut out of the factor markets and names the barriers precisely: no registered title means no collateral and therefore no loan; no information means tenders close unseen; apartheid settlement geography burns a heavy share of small wages on transport; and contracts travel along existing networks that newcomers penetrate slowly. Remedies pair with barriers: development finance through SEFA and the NYDA, tenure reform, incubators, learnerships and public transport investment. Community participation through ward committees and IDP forums makes economic sense because residents hold the local knowledge that lands a scarce budget where need binds tightest, and facilities a community chose are maintained rather than stripped. Empowerment procurement then adds the demand: the B-BBEE scorecard measures ownership, management control, skills development, enterprise and supplier development and socio-economic development, and the Preferential Procurement Policy Framework Act's 80/20 and 90/10 point systems award most points to price and a fixed remainder to transformation goals. Because the state is the largest single buyer in the economy, redirecting part of its purchasing redirects demand, and demand is what converts idle factors into factor incomes.
